advisor.summary: An HRA is an employer-funded plan reimbursing employees' medical care: the corporation deducts under §162(a), the employee excludes under §105(b) and §106(a), and nothing hits FICA. The C corporation is the uniquely clean chassis because its owner-employee is simply an employee — §1372 bars >2% S corporation shareholders from the same exclusion. The controlling hazard is the ACA market reforms: a standalone HRA covering two or more employees must be integrated with group coverage or fit a sanctioned design, on pain of the §4980D excise tax at $100 per employee per day, while a plan with fewer than two current-employee participants is exempt. Advisory-only — the benefit is a function of entity structure and actual medical spend, quantified in the plan design rather than modeled from return inputs.
mechanics: The corporation adopts a written reimbursement plan; payments of medical care described in §213(d) for the employee, spouse, and dependents are deductible under §162(a) and excluded from income and FICA wages under §105(b) and §106(a).

A C-corp owner-employee participates on the same footing as any employee — the double-tax structure that usually penalizes C corporations runs in the owner's favor here, converting family medical costs into corporate deductions with no shareholder-level income.
The same door is closed to pass-through owners: §1372 treats >2% S corporation shareholders as partners, so their reimbursements land on the W-2 and route through §162(l) rather than being excluded.

A standalone HRA covering two or more current employees violates the ACA market reforms unless integrated with group coverage or structured as a QSEHRA, ICHRA, or excepted-benefit HRA; a plan with fewer than two current-employee participants is exempt under §9831(a)(2), which is why owner-only C corporations implement this with minimal friction.
Self-insured nondiscrimination under §105(h) applies: an HRA favoring highly compensated individuals as to eligibility or benefits taxes the HCI's excess reimbursements.

authority.note: Excludes employer reimbursements of medical expenses of the employee, spouse, and dependents.
Excludes the employer-provided coverage itself from the employee's income.
The corporate deduction for reimbursements and plan costs as ordinary compensation expense.
Self-insured plan nondiscrimination; the discriminatory excess is taxable to highly compensated individuals.
Why S corporations fail here: >2% shareholders are treated as partners for fringe-benefit purposes.
The market-reform analysis: standalone HRAs covering two or more employees must integrate with group coverage or fit an excepted design.
The excise tax — $100 per affected employee per day — that backs the market-reform rules.
Exempts plans with fewer than two current-employee participants from the market reforms.
Defines the medical care an HRA may reimburse tax-free.

requirements: A C corporation with the owner as a bona fide W-2 employee.
A written plan document — covered class, annual limit, substantiation procedure — adopted before the first reimbursement.
A documented ACA compliance path: the one-participant exemption, integration with group coverage, or a sanctioned design.
Receipts or EOBs substantiating every reimbursement before payment.
§105(h) testing where the plan is self-insured and the corporation has a broader workforce.
risks: The dominant exposure is the §4980D excise tax — $100 per affected employee per day, $36,500 per employee per year — for a standalone design that fails the market reforms; Notice 2013-54 is the controlling ruling, and it is the reason the compliance path is designed before the plan rather than after.
§105(h) discrimination converts the owner's excess reimbursements into taxable income when a broader workforce is excluded.

Unsubstantiated or non-§213(d) reimbursements lose the exclusion, and a corporation with no business substance beyond paying the family's bills invites constructive-dividend recharacterization of the whole arrangement.
Do not let the HRA drive entity choice by itself — double taxation on remaining C-corp earnings can swamp the health benefit; run the full comparison.
Each new hire changes the plan's legal posture: the one-participant exemption is lost the day a second employee becomes eligible.
stateNotes: Conformity: states starting from federal AGI or federal taxable income conform to both the corporate deduction and the employee exclusion; no separate state filing position is required in conforming states.
PTET: none — the sponsor is a C corporation, so there is no pass-through entity tax interaction.
Missouri: conforms — the deduction runs through the Missouri corporate return's federal-taxable-income start (RSMo §143.431) and the exclusion stays out of Missouri AGI under RSMo §143.121.
reviewChecklist: Written plan and board resolution executed and dated before any reimbursement.
ACA compliance path documented for the current participant count.
Substantiation process live — receipts or EOBs before payment, log maintained.
§105(h) analysis current for the census; owner-only status confirmed where the exemption is relied on.
Modeled savings, if presented, tie to actual family medical spend rather than the plan cap.

client.teaser: Your corporation can repay your family's medical bills — deductible to it, tax-free to you.
client.headline: Let your corporation pay the medical bills you already have
plainEnglish: If your business is a regular C corporation, it can adopt a formal plan to repay employees for medical costs — doctor visits, prescriptions, dental, vision, deductibles. The company deducts those payments. The employee pays no tax on them.

Here is the key: as an owner who works in the company, you are one of those employees. Bills your family pays anyway, with already-taxed money, can be paid by the company with money that is never taxed.

Health-care law tightly controls how these plans are built, and the penalty for a sloppy one is severe. So the paperwork comes first, the payments second. We design the plan, put the documents in place, and keep the records clean.
client.analogy: It is like a standing discount on every medical bill equal to your tax rate — the money that pays the doctor never passes through your taxable income.
benefits: Family medical costs become company deductions
Reimbursements reach you free of income and payroll tax
Covers what insurance misses — deductibles, dental, vision
Repeats every year the plan stays in place
steps: WE confirm your structure qualifies and pick the compliant plan design.
WE draft the written plan before any money moves.
YOU submit receipts; the company reimburses you.
WE reconcile the plan and the deduction at year-end.
clientCommitments: Submit a receipt or insurance statement for every reimbursement — no receipt, no payment
Tell us before hiring — a second employee changes the plan rules
Run reimbursements from the company account, never as informal transfers

annualMaintenance: Annual §105(h) re-test as the census changes
Year-end reconciliation of reimbursements, substantiation, and the Form 1120 deduction
deliverables: Written HRA plan document and adopting resolution
Substantiation log and reimbursement request templates
